title: Why are football cards red and yellow? Blame a traffic light
description: Football’s red and yellow cards began with a communication problem and a traffic light. Discover Ken Aston’s idea and what the two colours actually mean.

cover.alt: Plain yellow and red referee cards and a silver whistle rest on a violet notebook beside a football pitch
cover.credit: AI-generated illustrative cover created for BrainiLab; not an archival photograph or objects known to have belonged to Ken Aston.

practice: Discover more small details behind big games in the Sports Quiz.

sections.title: A traffic signal in the referee’s pocket
sections.html:
Football’s yellow and red cards were inspired by traffic lights: yellow communicates a caution; red communicates a sending-off. The colours give players and spectators a visible signal without relying on a shared language.

For such a dramatic little rectangle, the idea had a surprisingly ordinary starting point: a London road.

sections.title: A message lost at Wembley
sections.html:
FIFA’s account traces the problem to the 1966 World Cup. During England’s quarter-final against Argentina, referee Rudolf Kreitlein sent off Antonio Rattín. They spoke different languages, and the argument left onlookers confused.

Ken Aston, who chaired the referees’ committee, wanted a clearer way to communicate decisions. In London, a traffic light changing from yellow to red gave him the idea.

sections.title: The idea arrived before the cards
sections.html:
The cards were introduced at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico, four years after the tournament that inspired them.

That is the neat distinction for a quiz: 1966 for the inspiration, 1970 for their World Cup introduction. The colourful solution did not appear during the original argument.

sections.title: Does yellow always come first?
sections.html:
No. Under the IFAB’s Law 12, a second caution in the same match is a sending-off offence. But serious foul play or violent conduct can bring a straight red; a player does not need an earlier yellow.
